source: Siegert (2013) Variance estimation for Brier Score decomposition
finding: Brier score splits as Br = REL - RES + UNC. UNC is the Brier score of always forecasting the base rate. A useful forecast has Br below UNC, so resolution must exceed the reliability error.
numbers: Equation Br = REL - RES + UNC; UNC = Brier of the climatological mean.
quote: A `useful' forecast should have a Brier Score that is lower than its uncertainty component
limits: Decomposition is for the expectation; empirical estimates need binning.
agent_relevance: S9 class record: log REL, RES and UNC per question class, not only the total Brier.

source: Siegert (2013) Variance estimation for Brier Score decomposition
finding: The standard (Murphy) component estimators are biased. Ferro and Fricker (2012) showed this and gave corrected estimators that reduce but never remove the bias. Siegert derives sampling variances for both versions.
numbers: Bias-corrected estimators have larger variance than the traditional ones (shown on artificial data and a weather example).
limits: Bias correction trades bias for variance; small classes stay noisy.
agent_relevance: With few resolved items per class, component estimates in the S9 record are unreliable. Report counts and intervals, and use the total Brier for small classes.

source: Ferro and Fricker (2012) A bias-corrected decomposition of the Brier score
finding: Reported via Siegert and a search abstract (full text not opened): standard decomposition estimators are biased in large samples. Reliability tends to be overestimated, uncertainty underestimated, resolution either way. An unbiased decomposition is unattainable; a lower-bias one is proposed.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Second-hand; PDF download failed.
agent_relevance: Treat per-class REL numbers as upward biased when classes are small.

source: Jewson (2004) The problem with the Brier score
finding: Brier can prefer a catastrophic forecast. Example: f1 = 0 always versus f2 = 0.25, with the event occurring 10% of the time. Brier prefers f1 by 1/80 (1/16 - 1/20), though f1 is wrong with certainty whenever the event happens.
numbers: Brier difference 1/80 in favour of f1; event frequency 1 in 10.
quote: Forecast f1 is a disaster: it predicts a zero probability
limits: Argument by intuition, not proof. Recommends a log-type score instead.
agent_relevance: Brier is lenient on confident misses. For rare high-stakes events, also log the log score and the worst single miss.

source: Gneiting and Raftery (2007) Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation
finding: A rule is proper if the forecaster maximises expected score by reporting the true belief; strictly proper if that is unique. Logarithmic, spherical, pseudospherical and quadratic (Brier) scores are strictly proper.
numbers: Review; abstract and introduction read, theory sections not checked line by line.
quote: A scoring rule is proper if the forecaster maximizes the expected score for an observation drawn from the distribution F if he or she issues the probabilistic forecast F
limits: Propriety does not say which proper rule suits a task; rules can rank forecasters differently.
agent_relevance: Use only strictly proper rules for any training signal or logged grade. Accuracy percent is improper for probabilities.

source: Hoessly (2025) On misconceptions about the Brier score in binary prediction models
finding: Lists five misconceptions. A Brier of 0 implies extreme 0/100% forecasts. Lower Brier is only comparable on the same population. A low Brier does not mean good calibration. A score near mean(y)(1-mean(y)) does not mean useless. The score can exceed that threshold by chance.
numbers: Table 1, five misconceptions; threshold is base rate times (1 - base rate).
limits: Written for clinical models; no empirical study.
agent_relevance: Never compare Brier across question classes with different base rates. Compare to the class's own UNC or to a base-rate forecast.

source: Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deep nets are miscalibrated, worse than older small nets. Temperature scaling (one parameter fitted on a validation set) fixes most of it and beat richer methods on vision tasks.
numbers: ECE (15 bins): CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53% to 1.26% after scaling; CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 4.6% to 0.83%; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48% to 1.86%.
limits: Classification nets; ECE depends on bin count; scaling needs held-out labelled data and assumes no shift.
agent_relevance: A cheap post-hoc recalibration map fitted on logged forecasts is a credible fix for the agent. It needs enough resolved items.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Temperature scaling did not help everywhere. On LeNet 5 CIFAR-100 ECE rose from 4.85% to 6.48%, and on text datasets it only matched other methods.
numbers: LeNet 5 CIFAR-100: 4.85% before, 6.48% after (first column of table is uncalibrated, second is temperature scaling).
limits: One of few counter-cases; column reading from a text extraction of the table.
agent_relevance: Recalibration can hurt on small or already-calibrated models; check on a holdout.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large pretrained LMs are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false in the right format. Calibration improves with model size and from 0-shot to few-shot. P(True) self-evaluation of a sampled answer also improves with size and with seeing several samples.
numbers: Binary chance Brier = 0.25. ECE uses 10 equal-count bins.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format
limits: Pretrained models, not RLHF. Trained P(IK) calibrates poorly on new tasks.
agent_relevance: Self-probability may be a usable signal for a base model; do not assume it for tuned assistants.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Preference-trained (RLHF) policies look very miscalibrated, but one fixed temperature (T = 2.5) largely repairs it on several tasks.
numbers: Single T = 2.5 for all evaluations.
limits: Quick side experiment; authors say heavier RL may distort calibration beyond repair.
agent_relevance: Post-training damage to probabilities may be undone by a simple fitted transform.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF models, stated confidence in numbers or words is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several answers first improves it more.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo SciQ ECE: label prob 0.219 vs verbalised top-4 0.056. TruthfulQA ECE: 0.445 vs 0.198. TriviaQA ECE: 0.078 vs 0.024 to 0.041. Abstract: ECE cut by relative 50% or more.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Gain is mostly ECE; AUC (discrimination) changes little. The paper notes a constant 50% guesser has perfect ECE on binary tasks.
agent_relevance: Ask for a probability on API-only models. Judge it on a proper score plus discrimination, never ECE alone.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: Calibration varies by dataset and model. TruthfulQA stayed poorly calibrated for conditional probabilities (ECE 0.445 for gpt-3.5). Claude-2 had weaker conditional probabilities than Claude-1 and GPT models, yet its verbalised calibration was consistently better.
numbers: See ECE numbers in the previous Tian line.
limits: Three QA datasets; grading free-form correctness is itself hard.
agent_relevance: Calibration is task-specific: keep per-class records, as S9 intends.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty?
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident, often piling on multiples of 5. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model size, but even GPT-4 averages AUROC of only 62.7%. Prompting (human-style, multiple samples, aggregation) reduces overconfidence in part. No method wins everywhere.
numbers: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-3 to GPT-4 AUROC up about 22.2%. White-box 0.605 AUROC vs 0.522 verbalised.
quote: LLMs tend to be highly overconfident when verbalizing their confidence
limits: Worst on professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics).
agent_relevance: Stated probability separates right from wrong poorly; a code check should outweigh stated confidence (G5).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: The best retrieval-and-fine-tuned system nears but does not beat the human crowd. Base models without retrieval sit near the 0.25 coin-flip line.
numbers: Test set: system Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%). Best zero-shot baseline GPT-4-1106 0.208. Random 0.250.
limits: Crowd leads when it is very confident (below 0.05); system hedges. Questions after the model cutoff only.
agent_relevance: A .03 Brier gap is what 'near human' means. Read our benchmark numbers against crowd and base rate.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Ablations: fine-tuning and retrieval matter; prompt search gives a small gain. No fine-tuning: .186 (+.007). Neither fine-tuning nor retrieval: .206, back at the baseline. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 gets .182.
numbers: Full .179; no fine-tune .186; neither .206; GPT-3.5 version .182.
limits: Differences of .003-.007 sit near the standard errors (.002-.003).
agent_relevance: Information (retrieval) matters more than prompt wording; spend scaffold effort on evidence.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Where the crowd is unsure (0.3-0.7) the system beats it. The system hedges even when evidence turns decisive, which costs resolution. With 5 or more relevant articles it nears the crowd. Averaging system and crowd was best in every setting.
numbers: Crowd-uncertain subset: system .199 vs crowd .246.
limits: Training kept outputs that beat the crowd, which may leak crowd information.
agent_relevance: Hedging is a resolution problem, visible only in a decomposition. A reason S9 should log RES.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: A median of 12 LLMs matched a human tournament crowd on 31 binary questions. The models showed acquiescence: mean forecasts above 50% though outcomes were near even.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 baseline, t(30) = -2.35, p = 0.026; vs 925-person human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60) = 0.19, p = 0.850.
limits: Only 31 questions; no difference is not proof of equality. Preregistered main test.
agent_relevance: Aggregating models cancels some bias, but G4 holds: same-family samples are not independent.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: Showing models the human median improved accuracy, but a plain average of model and human forecast beat the model's own updated forecast.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p = 0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p < 0.001). Updated forecasts worse than the simple average: GPT-4 0.13 (t(92) = 2.583, p = .011), Claude 2 0.14 (t(92) = 3.530, p = .001).
limits: Study 2 only; two models.
agent_relevance: When a trusted external number exists, average it in by code instead of letting the model reword it (G5).

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Superforecasters beat the public and every LLM on a dynamic benchmark. Top LLMs saw the crowd forecast on market questions; the best LLM without it was worse.
numbers: 200-question subset: superforecaster median Brier 0.096, public 0.121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p < 0.001 vs superforecasters). Best LLM without crowd access 0.136.
limits: Superforecaster panel n = 39; 2024 models; mixed market and dataset questions.
agent_relevance: Reference point for our logs: the gap to superforecasters was about 0.026 even for the best model with crowd access.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Combination questions widen the gap. On the larger set superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. The 0.054 gap is bigger than the 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Combination questions need dependence handling.
agent_relevance: Logical coherence across linked questions is a weak spot; check it in code.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Brier falls roughly log-linearly with model strength. Extrapolation puts parity with superforecasters near Arena score 1406 or about 6.5e26 training FLOP.
limits: Few models; very wide intervals; extrapolation.
agent_relevance: Do not plan on scaling alone; scaffold design is the lever we control.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Logical-consistency scores, computable now without ground truth, correlate with later Brier scores. Conditional-probability checks reach R above 0.9; other checks carry little signal. Part of the link is that better models are better at both.
numbers: Best checks R > 0.9; MMLU error vs Brier correlation 0.38 (NewsAPI) and 0.55 (scraped).
limits: Few forecasters tested; forecasters worse than random excluded; correlation not causation.
agent_relevance: An instant label-free check: log coherence violations in S9 beside Brier.

source: Hambly et al. (2025) Bench to the Future
finding: A pastcasting setup (resolved questions plus frozen web corpus) tracks model progress. Newer Claude models score better, but many pairs are not significantly different. Thinking mode did not help.
limits: Authors say absolute Briers are hard to interpret; effective sample about 179 questions after weighting; leak risk.
agent_relevance: Small samples cannot rank close models; do not read thinking-mode gains from small Brier differences.

source: Hambly et al. (2025) Bench to the Future
finding: Because outcomes are known, pastcasting needs leak control. The authors down-weight questions correlated by construction and drop rare odd cases (0.003%).
numbers: Effective sample 178.8 questions.
limits: Not a replacement for live resolution.
agent_relevance: Test scaffold changes on pastcasts first, then confirm live.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning about uncertainty: calibration of reasoning models
finding: Reasoning models are typically overconfident (stated confidence often above 85% even when wrong) and get more overconfident as reasoning effort rises. Introspection on their own trace helps o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 but made Claude 3.7 Sonnet worse.
numbers: Confidence above 85% (5% steps) on wrong answers; effect grows with reasoning effort.
quote: reasoning models ... become even more overconfident with deeper reasoning
limits: Question-answer tasks, not forecasting; few models.
agent_relevance: More thinking does not buy calibration; recalibrate outputs afterwards.

source: Murphy (1973) A new vector partition of the probability score
finding: Founding paper of the REL-RES-UNC split. Cited, not opened; content known only through Siegert and a search summary.
numbers: None read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Cite Siegert for formulas.

source: Brier (1950) Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability
finding: Original quadratic score for probability forecasts. Cited by Siegert, Jewson and Hoessly; not opened.
numbers: None read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Definitions only.
